subject: Critical Thinking
title: Why Every Decision Is a Bet
description: A quick win: understand Why Every Decision Is a Bet.

hook.text: You choose a restaurant without reading reviews. You take a job without knowing the boss.

buildup.text: Annie Duke, former poker champion: every decision is a bet on an uncertain future with incomplete information.

discovery.text: We can't eliminate uncertainty — only manage it. Good decisions can have bad outcomes. Bad decisions can get lucky.

twist.text: Judging decisions by outcomes is the 'resulting' fallacy. A good bet can lose. That doesn't make it a bad bet.

climax.text: Decision quality and outcome quality are different. Focus on the process, not just the result.

punchline.text: You can't control outcomes. You can control how you decide.

quiz.question: What is the 'resulting' fallacy?
options: Judging a decision only by its outcome instead of its process
Making decisions based on results alone

details.summary: Annie Duke argues that every decision is a bet on an uncertain future. Thinking of decisions as bets forces you to estimate probabilities, consider what you might be wrong about, and accept that good decisions can have bad outcomes.
details.whyItMatters: Framing decisions as bets separates decision quality from outcome quality, which is essential for learning from experience accurately.
takeaways: Decisions are bets on uncertain outcomes
Good decisions can produce bad outcomes and vice versa
Thinking in bets reduces emotional attachment to outcomes

faq.question: How does treating decisions as bets improve decision quality?
faq.answer: It forces you to estimate probabilities, explicitly acknowledge uncertainty, and separate the quality of your reasoning from the luck of the outcome. This prevents both overconfidence and result-oriented thinking.

faq.question: What is the difference between a bad decision and a bad outcome?
faq.answer: A bad decision uses poor reasoning or ignores available evidence. A bad outcome can follow a good decision due to luck. Poker illustrates this: you can play perfectly and still lose a hand. The goal is better processes, not guaranteed results.
